From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
(Redirected from [List of selected stars for navigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_selected_stars_for_navigation&redirect=no "List of selected stars for navigation"))
[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/DN-SD-03-08769.JPEG/250px-DN-SD-03-08769.JPEG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DN-SD-03-08769.JPEG)
The selected stars for navigation are often used for [sextant observations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextant_observation "Sextant observation").
*The selected stars for navigation are often used for sextant observations.*
Fifty-seven navigational [stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star "Star") and additionally the star [Polaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polaris "Polaris") are given a special status in the field of [celestial navigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_navigation "Celestial navigation"). Of the approximately six thousand stars visible to the [naked eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naked_eye "Naked eye") under optimal conditions, these selected stars are among the brightest and span thirty-eight [constellations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constellation "Constellation") of the [celestial sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_sphere "Celestial sphere") from the [declination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declination "Declination") of −70° to +89°. Many of the selected stars were named in [antiquity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_history "Ancient history") by the [Babylonians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylonia "Babylonia"), [Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks "Greeks"), [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_people "Roman people"), [Arabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs "Arabs") and [Polynesians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesians "Polynesians")[\[1\]](#cite_note-1).
The star [Polaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polaris "Polaris"), often called either the "Pole Star" or the "North Star", is treated specially due to its proximity to the north [celestial pole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_pole "Celestial pole"). When navigating in the [Northern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere "Northern Hemisphere"), a simple and quick technique can be used with Polaris to determine the observers [latitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latitude "Latitude") or, for larger maritime vessels can be used to calculate any [gyrocompass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyrocompass "Gyrocompass") error that may exist. The other fifty-seven selected stars have daily positions given in [nautical almanacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautical_almanac "Nautical almanac"), aiding the [navigator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_mate "Second mate") in efficiently performing observations on them. A second group of 115 "tabulated stars" can also be used for celestial navigation, but are often less familiar to the navigator and require extra calculations.
Although [Polaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polaris "Polaris") can quickly and simply give a solution for latitude in the northern hemisphere, it can not participate in giving a position fix including longitude - it is for this reason it is excluded from the list of 57 primary navigational stars, each of which can be used to produce (in conjunction with each other, known time in relation to the prime meridian and a set of sight reduction tables) an actual latitudinal and longitudinal positional fix.
For purposes of identification, the positions of navigational stars — expressed as declination and [sidereal hour angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidereal_hour_angle "Sidereal hour angle") — are often rounded to the nearest degree. In addition to tables, [star charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_chart "Star chart") provide an aid to the navigator in identifying the navigational stars, showing [constellations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constellation "Constellation"), relative positions, and brightness.
In practical use for sight reductions whilst at sea, tables can further assist a navigator by giving approximate altitudes (angles above the horizon) and azimuths (degrees as read from the compass) from an assumed or estimated position, usually helping to quickly determine the location and then quickly identify a particular navigational star that may be useful for a sight reduction.
## Background
\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_stars_for_navigation&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")\]
[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Nautical_almanac_left-hand_page.png/250px-Nautical_almanac_left-hand_page.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nautical_almanac_left-hand_page.png)
Selected navigation stars (except Polaris) listed on a [U.S. Nautical Almanac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautical_almanac "Nautical almanac") page for May 1995
*Selected navigation stars (except Polaris) listed on a U.S. Nautical Almanac page for May 1995*
Under optimal conditions, approximately six thousand stars are visible to the naked eye of an observer on Earth.[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002249-2) Of these, fifty-eight stars are known in the field of navigational astronomy as "selected stars", including nineteen stars of the [first magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-magnitude_star "First-magnitude star"), thirty-eight stars of the second [magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnitude_\(astronomy\) "Magnitude (astronomy)"), and [Polaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polaris "Polaris").[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002249-2) The selection of the stars is made by [His Majesty's Nautical Almanac Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/His_Majesty's_Nautical_Almanac_Office "His Majesty's Nautical Almanac Office") and the [US Naval Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Naval_Observatory "US Naval Observatory"), in the production of the yearly _[Nautical Almanac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautical_Almanac "Nautical Almanac")_ which the two organizations have published jointly since 1958.[\[3\]](#cite_note-USNO_almanac_history-3) Criteria in the choice of stars includes their distribution across the celestial sphere, brightness, and ease of identification.[\[4\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrightWhitney1992273-4) Information for another 115 stars, known as "tabulated stars", is also available to the navigator.[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002249-2) This list provides information on the name, approximate position in the celestial sphere, and [apparent magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apparent_magnitude "Apparent magnitude") of the 58 selected stars in tabular form and by star charts.
These stars are typically used in two ways by the navigator. The first is to obtain a [line of position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_of_position "Line of position") by use of a [sextant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextant "Sextant") observation and the techniques of celestial navigation.[\[5\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002301–303-5) Multiple lines of position can be intersected to obtain a position known as a celestial fix. The second typical use of the navigational stars is to determine gyrocompass error by computing the [azimuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azimuth "Azimuth") of a star and comparing it to an azimuth measured using the ship's gyrocompass.[\[6\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002271–274-6) Numerous other applications also exist.
Navigators typically refer to stars using one of two naming systems for stars: common names and [Bayer's designations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayer's_Name "Bayer's Name").[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002249-2) All of the selected stars have had a common name since 1953, and many were named in antiquity by the Arabs, Greeks, Romans, and Babylonians.[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002249-2) Bayer's naming convention has been in use since 1603, and consists of a Greek letter combined with the possessive form of the star's constellation.[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002249-2) Both names are shown for each star in the tables and charts below.
Each star's approximate position on the celestial sphere is given using the [equatorial coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_coordinate_system "Equatorial coordinate system"). The celestial sphere is an imaginary globe of infinite size with the Earth at its center.[\[7\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002234-7) Positions on the celestial sphere are often expressed using two coordinates: [declination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declination "Declination") and sidereal hour angle, which are similar to latitude and [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude "Longitude") on the surface of the Earth. To define declination, the Earth's [equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator "Equator") is projected out to the celestial sphere to construct the [celestial equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_equator "Celestial equator"), and declination is measured in degrees north or south of this celestial equator.[\[7\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002234-7) Sidereal hour angle is a measurement between 0° and 360°, indicating how far west a body is from an arbitrarily chosen point on the celestial sphere called the _[First Point of Aries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Point_of_Aries "First Point of Aries")_. Note that right ascension, as used by astronomers, is 360° minus the sidereal hour angle.
The final characteristic provided in the tables and star charts is the star's brightness, expressed in terms of apparent magnitude. Magnitude is a logarithmic scale of brightness, designed so that a body of one magnitude is approximately 2.512 times brighter than a body of the next magnitude.[\[Note 1\]](#cite_note-mag-8)[\[8\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002229-9) Thus, a body of magnitude 1 is 2.5125 (~100) times brighter than a body of magnitude 6.[\[9\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002219-10) The dimmest stars that can be seen through a 200-inch terrestrial telescope are of the 20th magnitude, and very bright objects like the Sun and a full Moon have magnitudes of −26.7 and −12.6 respectively.[\[9\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002219-10)

Navigators often use [star charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_chart "Star chart") to identify a star by its position relative to other stars. References like the _Nautical Almanac_ and _The American Practical Navigator_ provide four star charts, covering different portions of the celestial sphere. Two of these charts are [azimuthal equidistant projections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azimuthal_equidistant_projection "Azimuthal equidistant projection") of the north and south poles. The other two cover the equatorial region of the celestial sphere, from the declination of 30° south to 30° north. The two equatorial charts are [mercator projections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercator_projection "Mercator projection"), one for the eastern hemisphere of the celestial sphere and one for the western hemisphere. Note that unlike familiar maps, east is shown to the left and west is shown to the right. With this orientation, the navigator can hold the star chart overhead, and the arrangement of the stars on the chart will resemble the stars in the sky.[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowditch2002249-2)
In the star charts, constellations are labelled with capital letters and indicated by dotted lines collecting their stars. The 58 selected stars for navigation are shown in blue and labelled with their common name, star number, and a Greek letter to indicate their Bayer designation. The additional 115 tabulated stars that can also be used for navigation are shown in red and labelled with a Greek letter to indicate their Bayer designation. Some additional stars not suitable for navigation are also included on the charts to indicate constellations, they are presented as unlabelled small red dots.
### Equatorial stars
\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_stars_for_navigation&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Equatorial stars")\]
**Equatorial stars of the eastern hemisphere**
The equatorial region of the celestial sphere's eastern hemisphere includes 17 navigational stars from Alpheratz in the constellation Andromeda to Denebola in Leo. It also includes stars from the constellations Cetus, Aries, Taurus, Orion, Canis Major and Minor, Gemini, and Hydra. Of particular note among these stars are "the dog star" Sirius, the brightest star in the sky, and four stars of the easily identified constellation Orion.

**Equatorial stars of the western hemisphere**
The equatorial region of the celestial sphere's western hemisphere includes 12 navigational stars from Gienah in the constellation Corvus to Markab in Pegasus. It also includes stars from the constellations Virgo, Bootes, Libra, Corona Borealis, Scorpius, Ophiuchus, Sagittarius, and Aquila. The [variable star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_star "Variable star") Arcturus is the brightest star in this group.

The 11 northern stars are those with a declination between 30° north and 90° north. They are listed in order of decreasing sidereal hour angle, or from the [vernal equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox_\(celestial_coordinates\) "Equinox (celestial coordinates)") westward across the sky. Starting with Schedar in the constellation Cassiopeia, the list includes stars from the constellations Auriga, the Great and Little Bears, Draco, Lyra, and Cygnus. The two brightest northern stars are Vega and Capella.
In the star chart to the right, declination is shown by the radial coordinate, starting at 90° north in the center and decreasing to 30° north at the outer edge. Sidereal hour angle is shown as the angular coordinate, starting at 0° at the left of the chart, and increasing counter-clockwise.

The 18 southern stars are those with a declination between 30° south and 90° south. They are listed in order of decreasing sidereal hour angle, or from the [vernal equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox_\(celestial_coordinates\) "Equinox (celestial coordinates)") westward across the sky. Starting with Ankaa in the constellation Phoenix, the list includes stars from the constellations Eridanus, Carina, Crux, Centaurus, Triangulum Australe, Scorpius, Sagittarius, Pavo, and Grus. Canopus, Rigil Kentaurus, Achernar, and Hadar are the brightest stars in the southern sky.
In the star chart to the right, declination is shown by the radial coordinate, starting at 90° south in the center and decreasing to 30° south at the outer edge. Sidereal hour angle is shown as the angular coordinate, starting at 0° at the right of the chart, and increasing clockwise.
### Planisphere
\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_stars_for_navigation&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Planisphere")\]
The _Star Finder 2102-D_ ([Weems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._V._H._Weems "P. V. H. Weems") & [Plath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plath_GmbH "Plath GmbH"), Inc., [NSN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_Stock_Number "NATO Stock Number"): 6605-00-129-6526) is a tool for celestial navigators in a form of standard pocket [planisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planisphere "Planisphere") (its double-sided 8½["](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inch "Inch")\-disk star chart includes all the 57 navigation stars[\[69\]](#cite_note-73)) with a set of 9 identifier transparent overlays per each 5°-latitude and one meridians overlay, based on the original _Rude Star Finder_ _and Identifier_ (patented by Gilbert T. Rude in 1920)[\[70\]](#cite_note-74) modified by E. B. Collins and [United States Hydrographic Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Hydrographic_Office "United States Hydrographic Office") (_Star-Finder 2021-B and 2102-C_ released in 1940s),[\[71\]](#cite_note-75)[\[72\]](#cite_note-76)[\[73\]](#cite_note-77) and further modified and published by the Simex Instruents, with recent modifications by the Weems & Plath.[\[74\]](#cite_note-78)[\[75\]](#cite_note-79)[\[76\]](#cite_note-80)[\[77\]](#cite_note-81)[\[78\]](#cite_note-82) Its use described in _The Star Finder Book: A Complete Guide to the Many Uses of the 2102-D Star Finder_ by David Burch.[\[79\]](#cite_note-83) Unlike other pocket planispheres, commonly used in [amateur astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_astronomy "Amateur astronomy"),[\[a\]](#cite_note-84)[\[80\]](#cite_note-85) the _Star Finder 2102-D_ disk star chart has only dots representing stars positions and size, labeled only with its common names, and no other info (such as constellation lines and names, grids, etc.), making it unusable without overlays set and data table.
